content: Some of the internal kinetic energy in amorphous substances exists in the form of interparticle bonds. When an interparticle chemical bond is broken, along with the associated strain-relieving local adjustments in the centers of vibration, a configuron is formed. A configuron represents an elementary configurational excitation within an amorphous material. Configurons are instrumental in understanding the transition of a material from a solid state to a fluid state with viscous flow. Amorphous substances lack translational periodicity, and their internal kinetic energy can be partially stored in interparticle bonds. The particles that constitute an amorphous substance can vary widely in size, ranging from subatomic particles like electrons to macroscopic entities such as stars in a galaxy or even galaxies within a galactic cluster. Water is an example of an amorphous substance that can also exist in a crystalline form. Amorphous substances undergo phase transitions, such as solid-to-liquid, solid-to-gas, liquid-to-gas, or gas-to-plasma. The chemical bonding within many amorphous substances often results in short-range order, even though long-range disorder is present. The short-range order is frequently characterized by symmetrical arrangements of polyhedra, while the long-range disorder can be described by disordered arrangements of space-filling polyhedra. These polyhedra are bonded together in the solid state and undergo bond breaking during transitions from solid to fluid states. A model based on configurons or configurational microstates provides a framework for understanding changes in viscosity as a function of temperature. The particles in an amorphous substance can include subatomic particles, atoms, ions, molecules, dust, crystallites, grains, stones, boulders, or larger debris. From the perspective of gravitational bonding, the universe itself can be considered an amorphous substance. Amorphous substances can fall into the conventional categories of solid, liquid, gas, or plasma. However, some amorphous substances, such as sand, behave as fluids. Liquid water, for instance, expresses much of its available kinetic energy through additional degrees of freedom compared to water vapor. Some of this energy is stored in the form of intermolecular bonds, which act as a resistance to flow. Water has a relatively low viscosity compared to other liquids, such as vegetable oil or motor oil. Viscous flow in amorphous materials, such as water, is a thermally activated process. The activation energy in the liquid state (QL), temperature (T), the molar gas constant (R), and a nearly constant parameter (AL) are factors that influence viscosity. The enthalpy of motion of broken hydrogen bonds (Hm) is also relevant. In principle, any liquid can be transformed into an amorphous solid if the cooling rate is sufficiently high. Rapid cooling reduces molecular mobility, and if the cooling rate exceeds the rate at which molecules can organize into a thermodynamically favorable crystalline state, an amorphous solid is formed. Due to entropy considerations, many polymers can form amorphous solids even at slower cooling rates. Conversely, if molecules have enough time to organize into a structure with twoor three-dimensional order, a crystalline or semi-crystalline solid is formed. Water, due to its small molecular size and ability to rearrange quickly, cannot easily form an amorphous state without specialized hyperquenching techniques. These techniques produce amorphous ice, which has a quenching rate comparable to that of metallic glasses. The concentration of configurons in an amorphous material increases with temperature, and higher configuron concentrations correspond to lower viscosity. When configurons form percolating clusters, an amorphous solid can transition to a liquid, facilitating viscous flow. Thermodynamic parameters of configurons can be derived from viscosity-temperature relationships. Amorphous solids, like liquids, exhibit a topologically disordered distribution of particles but possess the elastic properties of isotropic solids. The symmetry similarities between liquid and solid phases cannot fully explain the qualitative differences in their behavior. Due to the characteristics of chemical bonding, amorphous solids, such as glasses, exhibit a high degree of short-range order in terms of local atomic polyhedra. For example, the amorphous structure of glassy silica lacks long-range order but demonstrates local ordering in the tetrahedral arrangement of oxygen atoms around silicon atoms. One useful approach to understanding amorphous materials is to focus on their bond systems rather than the set of particles that constitute the substance. For each state of matter, a bond lattice model can be defined. The bond lattice of amorphous materials is a disordered structure. Furthermore, the bond lattices of amorphous solids and liquids may exhibit different symmetries, unlike the symmetry similarity of particles in liquid and solid phases. In an amorphous material, a given unit can be defined by its nearest neighbors, and its structure can be characterized by a distribution of Voronoi polyhedra that fill the space of the disordered material. Molecular dynamics simulations have shown that the difference between a liquid and a glass in an amorphous material arises from the formation of percolation clusters of broken bonds within the Voronoi network. The Hausdorff dimension generalizes the concept of dimensionality in real vector spaces. For example, the Hausdorff dimension of a point is zero, a line is one, a plane is two, and a solid is three. The Hausdorff dimension can be thought of as the power of radii for a set of space-filling balls. In three dimensions, these balls can be spheres of varying radii, with their volumes proportional to r³, resulting in a Hausdorff dimension of 3. In four dimensions, the balls are hyperspheres, and their volumes are proportional to r⁴, giving a Hausdorff dimension of 4. Fractals often have Hausdorff dimensions that exceed their topological dimensions. For instance, a two-dimensional fractal may have a Hausdorff dimension between 2 and 3. At the solid-liquid transition, symmetry changes are expressed as stepwise variations in the Hausdorff dimension for bonds, with each broken bond contributing to the change. The glass transition temperature of water is approximately 136 K (-137°C). Factors influencing the formation of amorphous ice include the presence of ingredients that form heterogeneous mixtures with water (e.g., in ice cream production), pressure (which can convert one form into another), and cryoprotectants that lower the freezing point and increase viscosity. Melting low-density amorphous ice (LDA) between 140 and 210 K reveals that it is more viscous than normal water but denser than ordinary ice. Amorphous ice is used in scientific experiments, particularly in electron cryomicroscopy of biomolecules, where individual molecules can be preserved for imaging in a state close to their liquid water configuration. Hydrated proteins can also be classified as glass-forming systems, although they deviate significantly from thermorheological simplicity. The viscosity of water can be calculated using parameters such as AL and QL and compared to experimentally determined values across a range of temperatures. Systematic deviations are observed at higher temperatures. Adding the configuron contribution to the calculated values improves the fit to liquid water viscosity data, suggesting that water vapor, like other gas molecules mixed into water, can also contribute to the observed behavior.
